newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS - Ship insurers unable to halt hull rates fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ship insurers unable to halt hull rates fall.

text.p: Marine insurers at their annual convention this week showed no signs of being able to halt a continuing slide in underwriting rates for ship hulls.

Despite calls on underwriters by marine insurance industry leaders to sell tightly written policies at sensible prices, most are succumbing to pressure to underwrite wide-ranging cover at low prices in an attempt to retain market share in a very competitive market.
They are also signing up clients to three and five year insurance policies, meaning insurers are exposed regardless of future claims experience. And yet the industy seems unable to react.
At the annual conference of the International Union of Marine Insurers in Oslo on Tuesday, a lone voice stood to try and bolster resistance.
Harry Keefe, senior underwriter of GRE Underwriting in New York, rose at the end of a three hour hull insurance session which had not addressed the main issue facing the industry.
In a short, emotional speech he said, "I feel like part of a herd thundering towards a precipice. But I am not a dumb animal, I am an intelligent human being with the ability to choose."
Keefe pledged himself to no longer following underwriting practices he knew to be wrong.

"I vow to stop writing multi-year policies with ridiculous adjustment clauses which guarantee a loss, to stop ignoring terrible loss experience because it's a large fleet of modern vessels, and to stop treating sub-standard ships as if they were top of the line," he said.

Keefe was greeted by applause, but when the audience was asked if another delegate would stand up and back the challenge, there was a long awkward pause, and no hull underwriter or insurer got on his feet. Lunch was called minutes later.
Several observers commented afterwards that the moment reflected the sense resignation marine insurers appear to have to the downward drive on rates.

John Hickey, hull committee chairman of the American Institute of Marine Underwriters, told Reuters, "We had just managed to get prices right, then some underwriters started saying 'Well, maybe that is a bit overpriced', and now no-one is able to stop the run."
"We might learn our lesson eventually, as our customers don't like rates going up and down. But it will take a couple of cycles yet," said Hickey, referring to the cyclical nature of insurance rates.
IUMI's hull committee chairman Peter Chrismas touched on the gravity of the situation when he addressed delegates earlier.

"Over capacity, internal market and intermarket competition, an over-abundance of cheap reinsurance and a desire to maintain premium volume makes 1996 look marginal at best. The prospects for 1997 look dismal," he said.
"One has to question the professionalism of a business that provides its services on such a widely fluctuating basis," he said.

According to figures published at the conference, marine insurance premiums totalled $16.3 billion in 1994, up from $14.5 billion in 1993. Hull business earned $5.6 billion, up from $5.1 billion in 1993.
But Keefe estimates that total hull rates have fallen 26.5 percent since their high-point in mid-1994, and some believe the real figure to be higher.

One Lloyd's of London marine underwriter who declined to be named summed up the situation, "It looks like once again we have been unable to manage the insurance cycle. No doubt once again we will have the same come-uppance. A series of major losses will occur, and we will get burned."
